How to Delete or Edit Your Own Google Review

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

You can edit or delete a Google review you wrote at any time, from a computer or from the Google Maps app on Android and iPhone, in less than a minute. Deletion is immediate and permanent: the text, the stars and any reply from the business disappear, and the business's average rating is recalculated.

Who can delete a review, and who cannot

Only the author of a review can delete it directly, from the same Google account used to publish it. A business owner cannot remove a customer's review, and Google removes reviews written by others only when they violate its policies. Reviews stay linked to the account even if you later change your profile name or photo, so older reviews can be found and deleted the same way.

This is why the question of how to delete your own Google review comes up so often in Italy, from both sides. Customers change their minds after a problem is resolved, or regret a review written in anger. Businesses, for their part, sometimes contact a customer to ask whether they would consider updating it. Both situations are legitimate, as long as the decision remains with the reviewer, a point covered in detail further down.

Deleting a review on a computer

On desktop the quickest route is through Google Maps, where all your contributions are collected in one place. Menu labels can vary slightly between versions, but the path is essentially the same.

  1. Open Google Maps in your browser and sign in with the account you used to write the review.
  2. Click your profile picture or the menu, then open "Your contributions" or your profile, and select the Reviews tab.
  3. Find the review, click the three-dot icon next to it and choose "Delete review".
  4. Confirm the deletion when Google asks.

The same three-dot menu offers "Edit review", which lets you change the text, the number of stars or the photos without removing the review altogether. You can also reach your review by searching for the business on Google, opening its reviews and locating yours, but going through your own profile avoids scrolling through hundreds of entries.

Deleting a review on Android and iPhone

In the Google Maps app the steps are almost identical on both systems: profile, reviews, menu, delete. The app must be signed in to the account that wrote the review.

Android

Open Google Maps, tap your profile picture in the top corner and choose your profile or contributions. Under Reviews, locate the one you want to change, tap the three dots beside it and select delete, then confirm. If you use several Google accounts on the phone, switch to the correct one first, because reviews written from a work account will not appear under a personal one.

iPhone and iPad

On iOS, open the Google Maps app rather than Apple Maps, since Apple Maps does not display Google reviews. Tap your profile picture, open your profile, go to Reviews, tap the three dots on the relevant review and choose delete. Users who prefer the browser can follow the desktop steps in Safari after signing in to Google.

What happens after you delete a review

Once confirmed, the review is gone for good. Google offers no recycle bin or undo option, so if you only want to soften it, editing is the better choice.

  • The text, star rating and photos attached to the review are removed from the business profile.
  • Any reply the business wrote to your review disappears with it.
  • The business's average rating is recalculated, although the change may take some time to show everywhere.
  • You can write a new review of the same place later, which will appear with a new date.

Deleting your whole Google account also deletes all your reviews. Conversely, if a review vanishes without any action on your part, it was most likely filtered by Google's automated systems, which is a different issue from deliberate deletion.

Editing instead of deleting

An edit is often the more honest option when the original experience was real but the situation has since changed. A guest whose complaint about a hotel in Florence was resolved quickly can keep the review, update the rating and add a sentence explaining how the business handled it.

Readers tend to trust a review that tells the full story more than a perfect five stars. For the business, an updated review showing a problem solved well can be more persuasive than a silent deletion, because it demonstrates how complaints are treated. When editing, keep the original facts accurate and add what changed, rather than rewriting the story: a review that jumps from one star to five without explanation can look suspicious to other readers. That is also why a careful public reply matters before any request is made; our article on replying to a negative review without making things worse explains how to open that conversation.

When a business asks you to change your review

Businesses may contact a customer, explain what they have done to fix the problem and politely ask whether the customer would consider updating or removing a Google review you wrote about them. What they may not do is pay, reward or pressure you into it.

What is acceptable

Resolving the complaint first, then sending a single courteous message that leaves the decision entirely to the customer, is within Google's rules. A refund or replacement should be offered because the problem was real, not on condition that the review disappears.

What crosses the line

Offering discounts, free services or money in exchange for deleting a negative review, or for changing it to five stars, breaches Google's policy against incentivised content. Under the Italian Consumer Code (Codice del Consumo), as amended following the EU Omnibus Directive, manipulating consumer reviews is also an unfair commercial practice that the competition authority (AGCM) can sanction. Repeated messages, threats of legal action against a truthful review, or contacting the reviewer's employer amount to pressure, and a reviewer facing them can report the situation to Google.

The rule is simple: a business can fix the problem and ask once, but the review belongs to the customer, and so does the decision to change it.

For companies, the sustainable approach is to earn better reviews rather than chase deletions, as described in our guide to collecting positive reviews within platform rules.
